sentences.text: Fossils indicate that this animal reached a length of between 2 and 3 meters.
The primary specimen consists of a right humerus along with six vertebrae, including three located before the sacrum and three that are partial.
A second find, cataloged as SAM-PKK10654, contains five vertebrae, including three in the neck region and two at the rear of the presacral series.
Some researchers suggest this creature might be the oldest known dinosaur, appearing roughly 15 million years before others like Herrerasaurus.
The vertebrae found before the sacrum in these specimens show a striking resemblance to those of the mysterious archosaur Teleocrater rhadinus.
The holotype was gathered in the 1930s from the Lifua Member of the Manda Formation in southern Tanzania by Francis Rex Parrington.
These remains were collected at the Parrington B36 locality near Lake Nyasa in the same region.
The bones were initially described in 1956 within a doctoral thesis and labeled Specimen 50b.
English paleontologist Alan J. Charig first named the specimen in that 1956 thesis.
Charig later used the name Nyasasaurus parringtoni in 1967 without a full description, which led to it being viewed as an invalid name.
A new description published in 2013 by Sterling Nesbitt and colleagues validated the name and changed the specific epithet to parringtoni.
This 2012 analysis included Charig as a posthumous co-author and officially confirmed the species.
The generic name honors Lake Nyasa, while the specific name pays tribute to Parrington.
Study of the upper arm bone reveals rapid bone growth characterized by interwoven fibers, numerous blood vessel channels, and few growth lines.
The internal structure of the bones resembles that of the primitive dinosaur Coelophysis more than that of dinosaur ancestors.
Scientists have tested dinosaur affinities based on a long deltopectoral crest on the humerus with a deviated upper part, a feature found only in dinosaurs.
Consequently, the animal is considered a basal dinosaur or one very close to them.
The taxon is confidently placed within Archosauria and Dinosauriformes, and possibly within Dinosauria.
It is also classified within the unranked order Dinosauromorpha.
Furthermore, it belongs to the unranked family Dinosauriformes.
However, the humerus does not share any unique traits exclusively with any other Triassic archosaur group.

A 2017 phylogenetic analysis by Matthew Baron, David B. Norman, and Paul Barrett suggested it might represent a derived sauropodomorph related to masospondylines like Massospondylus and Lufengosaurus.
The parent group for this animal is listed as Dinosauria.
Other studies can securely place it within Archosauria, Dinosauria, and possibly Dinosauriformes.
The animal lived approximately 243 million years ago during the Anisian stage of the Middle Triassic in what is now Africa.
If radiometric dating is correct, the creature would be Carnian in age, significantly reducing the time gap between it and other early dinosaurs.
A 1986 hypothesis suggested Nyasasaurus was a primitive prosauropod dinosaur, but this was disputed.
Not all paleontologists accept the younger Carnian age proposed for the formation containing Nyasasaurus.
The SHRIMP dating methods used to determine the age of the Río Seco de la Quebrada Formation have been criticized as less accurate than CA-TIMS dating.
It was suggested that Nyasasaurus was a primitive prosauropod dinosaur, but this hypothesis is questionable.
